title: Levey-Jennings Charts & Westgard Rules

references.label: CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

summary: A Levey-Jennings chart plots QC results over time against the established mean and standard deviation, and Westgard rules are a defined set of statistical rules applied to that chart's pattern to decide whether an analytical run is in control or must be rejected.
explanation: Each QC data point is plotted relative to the target mean, typically with lines at ±1, ±2, and ±3 standard deviations (SD) — concepts the laboratory's existing mean/SD entries already define generically, applied here specifically to ongoing run-to-run QC monitoring rather than a one-time calculation. Westgard rules examine patterns across one or more consecutive QC points (not just a single point in isolation) to catch both random error (a single wildly off point) and systematic error/trend (a gradual shift or consistent bias) that a single-point check alone would miss; commonly cited example rules include a single point exceeding ±3 SD (a strong 'reject' signal on its own), or multiple consecutive points trending in the same direction or clustered on the same side of the mean (suggesting a developing systematic problem even if no single point is extreme). The specific rule set and violation-response actions a laboratory applies are defined by its own QC procedure, informed by these established statistical principles rather than one universal fixed rule for every analyte.

comparison.left: A single point far outside the control limits (e.g. beyond ±3 SD)
A run of consecutive points shifted/trending the same direction
comparison.right: Suggests a developing, ongoing bias (e.g. reagent degradation, calibration drift)

commonMisconceptions: Treating a QC point within ±2 SD as automatically 'fine' without looking at the surrounding pattern — several consecutive points on the same side of the mean, even within 2 SD each, can indicate a developing systematic problem that a single-point check misses.
